figures.caption: RoboScope Kit connects Policies and benchmark adapters. figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Work distribution and worker recovery. Workers atomically claim queued items and publish partial progress or completed results. After a worker exit or allocator out-of-memory error, the Control Runtime requeues unfinished work, discards its partial records, and starts a replacement worker, which replays the item from its first episode. Only completed items enter aggregation. Policy-replica exit has a different failure boundary: it aborts the evaluation (Section 3.7).
figures.headline: Work items move from pending to running to completed, and a worker failure requeues unfinished items for replay.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 shows the item states and the recovery path.
Worker failures are recovered at work-item granularity (Figure 3).

figures.caption: Grid search and diagonal concurrency search on LIBERO-Long, one RTX 4090. Grid lines are full evaluations at fixed $K/g$, one launch per configuration, one line per replica count $g$, labelled at its end; the search path joins the steady-state probes in the order the search ran them, mean of three launches, with $g$ marked where no grid line has that replica count; filled triangles are probes the search kept and hollow triangles probes it rejected; the star is the formal run at the selected configuration (median of three). (a) CUDA MPS off, on the sweep host with a 20-core quota: the grid takes eighteen launches and 5.4 h of evaluation, the search seven probes and 8.4 min (median) and selects $K12/g3$, within 1.2% of the fastest grid configuration, $K16/g4$. With CUDA MPS on, on the cross-system host with 12 pinned cores, a further replica keeps paying off (Figure 7b): the search keeps $K16/g4$, which adds 8–9% over $K12/g3$, and stops because $K20/g5$ is predicted to exceed GPU memory.

abstract: Simulation benchmarks are the standard way to compare robot policies, but each benchmark brings its own evaluator, observation layout, and action convention, and evaluation is slow: 500 RoboTwin Easy episodes with one simulator and one model on one GPU take 359.7 minutes. Profiling the official StarVLA evaluator shows that simulation occupies CPU cores while the GPU averages 14.3% utilization. RoboScope Kit wraps each model once in a Python class called a Policy, and each benchmark once in an adapter around the benchmark’s own evaluator, so the benchmark’s rules and scoring stay unchanged. Scheduling runs simulator workers and Policy replicas as separate pools, sizes both from measured probes, and shards work deterministically across GPU instances; runtime optimization renders only the observations an action-chunk Policy reads. Adapters cover six benchmark families. On LIBERO-Long with a StarVLA checkpoint on one 48 GiB RTX 4090, the concurrency search selects twelve simulator workers sharing three Policy replicas, which evaluate 500 episodes 4.45$\times$ faster than the official StarVLA evaluation with equivalent success rates, 2.78$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 1.52$\times$ faster than vla-eval at its tuned configuration. With CUDA MPS, which lets the replicas run their kernels concurrently, the search selects sixteen workers sharing four replicas, 6.16$\times$ faster than StarVLA, 3.85$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 2.10$\times$ faster than vla-eval. On RoboTwin Easy, four GPUs with chunk-boundary observation complete the 500 episodes in 14.4 minutes, 25.04$\times$ faster than the single-GPU baseline, with identical success outcomes and terminal steps.

sections.body: The paper addresses repeated integration work and slow evaluation. Each model is wrapped once as a Policy class and each benchmark once as an adapter around its own evaluator. Simulator workers and Policy replicas run as separate pools, sized by a concurrency search. Runtime optimization renders only observations the Policy reads. Adapters cover six benchmark families. The introduction reports that 500 RoboTwin Easy episodes take 359.7 minutes with one simulator and one model on one GPU, and that on RoboTwin, four GPUs with chunk-boundary observation complete the 500 episodes in 14.4 minutes, 25.04$\times$ faster than the single-GPU baseline.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: RoboScope Kit wraps models and benchmarks once and separates simulator workers from model replicas to speed evaluation.

sections.body: Profiling 50 LIBERO-Long episodes on one RTX 4090 shows that simulation and per-step handling take 55% of evaluator time, and waiting for actions takes 26%. An inference takes 55 ms, of which 26 ms is GPU kernel execution. The GPU averages 14.3% utilization. The StarVLA RoboTwin checkpoint has chunk length $H=16$, yet the official evaluator renders all three cameras at every control step, so 15 of every 16 rendered observations are never read. The section also lists five design goals: unified, faithful, efficient, automatic, and scalable.
sections.heading: Background and Motivation
sections.headline: The official StarVLA evaluator leaves the GPU at 14.3% average utilization because simulation and per-step handling dominate CPU time.

sections.body: A Control Runtime schedules K simulator workers and g Policy replicas as separate process pools and collects one episode record per episode key. The concurrency search runs short probes that measure throughput, CPU cores, GPU utilization, and memory. The worker phase doubles K while throughput rises by at least 25%. The replica phase adds replicas and scales workers as K=rg, keeping a step while throughput rises by at least 3%. Probes fail on worker or out-of-memory errors, timeouts, or success below 85% of the first probe. Work is sharded across instances by index modulo N. Failed worker items are requeued and replayed, and a replica exit aborts the evaluation.
sections.heading: Design
sections.headline: The design separates simulator workers from Policy replicas and uses a diagonal search to size both from measured probes.

sections.body: The Control Runtime, simulator workers, and Policy replicas run as separate processes on one host and communicate over local Unix-domain sockets. Benchmark adapters build work items, start native rollouts, translate observations and actions, and parse results, while task setup, termination, and scoring stay in the benchmark's own evaluator. A new Policy subclasses `Policy` and implements `load` and `act`. Stateful Policies key state by `episode_id` because one replica serves several workers. The X-VLA Policy is given as a stateful example that declares a stride of 1 on every benchmark. The entry point can take a shard index and shard count for multi-instance runs.
sections.heading: Implementation
sections.headline: The implementation packages a Python Policy API, native benchmark evaluators, and a six-family adapter catalog that run as separate local processes.

sections.body: On LIBERO-Long with one RTX 4090, the search-selected configuration K12/g3 scores 89.9% against 90.2% for the official evaluation, a difference of $-0.3$ percentage points, which is within the $\pm 2$-point equivalence margin. With CUDA MPS, K16/g4 also scores 89.9%. Median evaluation time is 671 s against 2,990 s for StarVLA, 4.45$\times$ faster, and 485 s with MPS, 6.16$\times$ faster. On RoboTwin Easy, four GPUs with chunk-boundary observation complete the episodes 25.04$\times$ faster than the single-GPU baseline, with identical success outcomes and terminal steps. The search takes a median 506 s, which the paper reports separately from evaluation time.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: RoboScope Kit matches official LIBERO-Long outcomes and evaluates 4.45 times faster than StarVLA, and 6.16 times faster with CUDA MPS.

sections.body: The section groups prior work into benchmarks, evaluation pipelines, simulation engines, and policy interfaces. It cites XPolicyLab and RoboDojo as systems with integrate-once or heterogeneous parallel goals, and vla-eval and RLinf as batch-parallel evaluators. It states that RoboScope Kit adds separately sized pools, a measured concurrency search, and runtime optimization declared through the Policy's observation stride. It positions the separation of environment stepping from inference against distributed reinforcement learning systems such as SEED RL and Sample Factory, and notes that evaluation needs complete, reproducible episode records rather than learning sample throughput.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: The related work places the paper among evaluation harnesses and simulation engines that separate simulators from inference.

sections.body: The discussion reports that the 506-second diagonal search adds 75% to LIBERO-Long evaluation time, and that the system remains 2.42$\times$ faster than the official evaluation end to end. On a 100-episode RoboTwin Easy subset, the search takes about 60% of each launch. The section argues that reporting search and tuning time separately makes the trade-off visible, so automation pays off mainly on workloads long enough to amortize the search.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Search cost is large on short workloads, so reporting search time beside evaluation time shows when automation pays off.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes the profiling result, the single Policy and adapter interface, and the scheduling and runtime optimizations. A second replica lets twelve workers reach 4.76$\times$ the throughput of one worker and one replica. On LIBERO-Long, the search-selected configurations are 4.45$\times$ faster than the official evaluation with equivalent outcomes, and 6.16$\times$ with CUDA MPS. Four GPUs scale RoboTwin Easy at a parallel efficiency of 0.91. The text states that deterministic sharding extends an evaluation across GPU instances.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The system matches official outcomes and cuts evaluation time 4.45 to 6.16 times on LIBERO-Long, and 359.7 to 14.4 minutes on RoboTwin Easy.

sections.body: The appendix gives the Policy lifecycle methods in Table 2 and the canonical observation and action contracts for six benchmarks in Table 3. It describes the work-queue state machine and recorded artifacts. It lists LIBERO-Long and RoboTwin Easy workloads, StarVLA revisions, and baseline configurations. It documents the vla-eval and RLinf offline tuning runs in Tables 4 and 5, including the sampled-action behavior found in RLinf's StarVLA evaluation. It closes with the adapter catalog in Table 19 and the failure classification.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists Policy lifecycle methods, benchmark contracts, work-queue states, experimental details, tuning runs, and adapter catalog.
